Text Message Scams

TV Licensing Scam Text UK: Spot a Fake Licence SMS

Scammers are sending fake TV Licensing text messages to UK residents—here's how to tell if yours is real and what to do about it.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-04-24 · Updated 2026-08-01 · 9 min read

Quick answer: TV Licensing sends some genuine payment and Direct Debit texts, including payment links for some plans, but says it never texts to say you are entitled to a refund or asks for bank details by text. Do not use the message to verify itself: type tvlicensing.co.uk independently, sign in, and forward suspicious texts to 7726.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a fake TV Licensing text looks like

A TV Licensing scam text is a fake SMS built to look like TV Licensing, so that you follow its link and type card, bank, or personal details into a page criminals control. An example of the style is: TV Licensing: Your direct debit failed and your licence is no longer valid. Update your payment to avoid a £1,000 fine: tvlicence-renew.example.

The pretexts criminals borrow are a Direct Debit that failed, a licence that has expired, and a refund you are owed. The first two are the awkward part: TV Licensing genuinely texts Direct Debit customers about payment problems and genuinely sends renewal reminders, so those subjects do not identify a scam on their own. The refund offer is different - TV Licensing says it does not text to tell you that you are entitled to one.

A fake link opens a convincing TV Licensing-style page that captures whatever you enter. Because TV Licensing sends genuine texts, some of which contain payment links, neither the channel nor the presence of a link settles it. What settles it is checking the same claim with TV Licensing opened independently, rather than through the message.

Why these texts fool people

TV Licensing is familiar to many UK households, so a payment problem feels plausible, and the threat of a fine adds pressure. A refund offer works the other way, by lowering caution. The sender ID and the link can both be faked to look official. Sender addresses are an email question rather than a text one — our TV Licence Scam Email UK: How to Spot a Fake guide lists the addresses TV Licensing currently identifies as genuine.

What TV Licensing says about its own texts is narrower and more useful. It says it may text a payment-card customer to ask for a payment, link a Simple Payment Plan customer to its payment site, confirm a TVL Pay payment, warn a Direct Debit customer about a payment problem, remind you that a licence is due for renewal, ask a former payment-scheme customer to set up a new way to pay, or confirm contact and ask for feedback.

It says it will not text you an offer of a refund, will not ask for your bank details by text, and will not ask for personal details on its website before you have successfully signed in.

Signs a TV Licensing text is a scam

Warning signs include an unexpected refund claim, a request for bank details by text, or a site that asks for personal details before you have successfully signed in. A payment problem or link is not conclusive by itself; verify the same issue independently in your TV Licensing account.

Alongside those, weigh the pressure tactics rather than the subject line:

  • It threatens a fine, court, or an "enforcement officer" unless you act today.
  • It pairs a generic greeting with a very short deadline.
  • It asks you to reply with your full card number, bank details, or account credentials.
  • The claim matches nothing you can find when you open your own account independently.
  • It arrives from an odd number - though a familiar sender name proves nothing either way, because sender IDs can be spoofed.

An unfamiliar, misspelled or lookalike address is a warning. TV Licensing currently lists tvlicensing.co.uk, tvl.co.uk, spp.tvlicensing.co.uk and 75plan.tvlicensing.co.uk as genuine, but visible link text and sender details can be faked. Do not use the message to verify itself: type tvlicensing.co.uk independently and check your licence or payment plan there.

TV Licensing's own scam guidance says a genuine Simple Payment Plan text may link to tvl.co.uk/spppay, so an address you do not recognise is a prompt to check independently rather than a verdict on its own. Parking-fine texts use the same small-sum, short-deadline framing — see our parking fine scam text guide.

How the scam works, step by step

First, a text claims a licence or payment problem, or a refund. Second, urgency - a fine or a deadline - pushes you towards the link. Third, a copy of the TV Licensing site asks for card and personal details, typically before any sign-in. Fourth, criminals use them for card fraud, bank fraud, or identity theft. Fifth, a phone call may arrive soon afterwards from someone claiming to be TV Licensing or your bank and quoting the details you just gave.

Opening tvlicensing.co.uk yourself interrupts that sequence at the second step - and it is the right move whether the original message was genuine or not.

How to check a TV Licensing text safely

Do not tap the link or call a number from the text. You can deal with the issue through your account instead of using the message's link.

  • Type tvlicensing.co.uk into your browser yourself, or sign in from a bill or letter you already have.
  • Check your licence status, payment plan, and any outstanding payment there, not through the link.
  • Expect to sign in first. TV Licensing says its missed-payment route asks for card details only after you have signed in with your licence number, last name, and postcode.
  • A no-licence conviction can lead to a fine of up to £1,000. If a court has fined you, use the payment instructions from the court, not a link in a message claiming to be TV Licensing.
  • Do not enter card, bank, or personal details on a page you opened from the message.
  • If you are unsure, contact TV Licensing through the contact options published on tvlicensing.co.uk.

If you are unsure whether a linked page is genuine, our guide on Is This Website a Scam? A Practical Checklist Before You Buy helps, our TV Licence Scam Email UK: How to Spot a Fake guide covers the same scam by email, and TV Licence Scam Letter UK: Spot a Fake Demand covers it by post.

What to do if you tapped the link or typed details

What you do next depends on what the page captured, so work through whichever of these describes your situation.

  • Card number typed in: phone the card issuer on the number printed on the card, have it secure or replace the card, and have it review recent spending for anything you did not authorise. A dispute route such as chargeback only becomes relevant if an eligible transaction was actually taken or later shows up - ask the issuer which route fits.
  • Online banking credentials typed in: speak to the bank through a route you already trust, such as its app or the number on a statement, and do what it tells you.
  • A password typed in: reset it inside the genuine service, and reset it anywhere else you reused it.
  • Anything installed or granted: if the page pushed a download, added an app or configuration profile, requested remote access, or the handset has misbehaved since, cut the connection to that session and work through the NCSC's current advice on responding to phishing and recovering a device.
  • If identity documents or personal information were exposed, review Cifas's current eligibility wording. Cifas says Protective Registration is only for people whose identities are at heightened risk. It places a warning flag that prompts extra checks on applications; it does not protect existing card transactions and is not insurance.

Our scam recovery checklist puts these in order alongside the money and account steps.

How to report a TV Licensing scam text (UK)

TV Licensing's FAQ 288 currently shows two different spellings for its screenshot-reporting mailbox, so this guide does not ask readers to choose between them. Forward suspicious SMS to 7726. If you also want to send TV Licensing a screenshot, contact it through its official Contact Us page and ask which current route to use. TV Licensing asks for suspicious emails to go to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk instead.

For WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal, preserve the evidence and use the app's report and block tools; 7726 is not the in-app reporting route.

If you lost money or shared sensitive information, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. It also has a route for reporting something suspicious where nobody responded and no money was lost, so a suspicious text is still worth reporting. Take a screenshot and note the sender before you report or delete the message.

Frequently asked questions

Does TV Licensing send texts, or is every TV Licensing text a scam?

TV Licensing sends genuine payment, Direct Debit, renewal and account-service texts, and some include links. It says it never texts to tell you that you are owed a refund, never asks for bank details by text, and does not ask for personal details until you have signed in. Verify the message independently at tvlicensing.co.uk.

A text says my TV Licence direct debit failed and I'll be fined - is it real?

It could be either. TV Licensing does text Direct Debit customers about payment problems, so the subject alone does not answer the question. Open tvlicensing.co.uk independently instead of tapping the link and see whether the same payment problem shows on your account. A no-licence conviction can lead to a fine of up to £1,000. If a court has fined you, use the payment instructions from the court, not a link in a message claiming to be TV Licensing.

The text offers a TV Licensing refund - should I claim it?

No. TV Licensing says it does not text to tell you that you are entitled to a refund, which makes an unexpected refund text one of the few subjects that is a warning sign in its own right. If you think a refund is genuinely due, open tvlicensing.co.uk independently and check it in your account.

I entered my card details on a TV Licensing-looking site - what now?

Phone the card issuer straight away on the number printed on the card, have the card secured or replaced, and have recent spending reviewed for anything you did not authorise; ask the issuer which dispute route fits any transaction that was actually taken. Reset any password you typed in, and any password you reused elsewhere. If the page pushed a download, added an app or profile, or asked for remote access, follow the NCSC's current device-recovery advice. Consider Cifas Protective Registration only where the exposure puts your identity at heightened risk; check Cifas's current criteria. Our scam recovery checklist sets out the order.

How do I report a TV Licensing scam text?

For an SMS, forward the message to 7726. For WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal, preserve the evidence and use the app's report and block tools; 7726 is not the in-app reporting route. If you also want to send TV Licensing a screenshot, take the mailbox from its current scam advice page or Contact Us route, because FAQ 288 currently shows two different spellings. If money was taken or you handed over sensitive details, add a report to Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.
